1 │ # Paging output can keep colour codes when I asked for none, can close my terminal output, and can fail on non-English text
   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ When I ask Click to send my long output through a pager, the colour cleanup only happens when a pager program is really running. If no pager is found, or my output is not going to a terminal, Click writes the text out as-is and the colour codes stay in the text, even though I asked for plain text. The same page-through helper also hands me back a stream that sits on top of my normal output, so if that stream gets closed, my usual output is closed with it and later prints fail. On Windows, and on the no-pager path everywhere, the text is written to a temporary file using whatever character set the machine happens to use, so text my terminal can display can still raise an encoding error there.
   6 │ 
   7 │ ## What should happen
   8 │ 
   9 │ Asking for plain output means plain output on every paging path, including the fallback that writes straight to the terminal. Closing what the pager gives me must never close my own output stream. The temporary-file path should write text the same way the pipe path does, using the encoding that matches my output and swapping out characters it cannot represent instead of failing.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## About this project
  12 │ 
  13 │ Click is a Python library for building command line programs. It gives you commands, options, prompts, progress bars, and helpers such as sending long output to a pager like less or more. The pager helper is what makes long help text or long reports easy to scroll through.
  14 │ 
  15 │ ## Problem this solves
  16 │ 
  17 │ I build tools that print long reports, and I need the output to stay readable when it is piped into a file or a log. Right now I get stray colour codes in my saved files, and on Windows my script can crash on text that works everywhere else, so I have to keep text ASCII-only as a workaround.
  18 │ 
  19 │ ## What changed
  20 │ 
  21 │ Colour codes are now removed on the no-pager path too, matching the running-pager path, so the colour setting is honoured everywhere. The stream the pager hands back no longer closes the output underneath it when it is closed itself. The temporary-file path now writes with the same encoding as the pipe path and replaces characters it cannot encode rather than raising an error.
  22 │ 
  23 │ ## Impact
  24 │ 
  25 │ Correctness and reliability: plain output is guaranteed on every paging path, my own output stream is safe from being closed, and non-English text no longer fails on Windows.
  26 │ 
  27 │ ## User experience
  28 │ 
  29 │ Before: I run my program with colours turned off and redirect the output to a file. The file contains stray escape sequences that make it look messy, and on Windows the same run can stop with an encoding error on accented or non-Latin characters. After: the saved file is clean plain text, my program's normal output keeps working after the pager finishes, and the same accented or non-Latin text is written out fine on Windows.

   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ When I ask Click to send my long output through a pager, the colour cleanup only happens when a pager program is really running. If no pager is found, or my output is not going to a terminal, Click writes the text out as-is and the colour codes stay in the text, even though I asked for plain text. The same page-through helper also hands me back a stream that sits on top of my normal output, so if that stream gets closed, my usual output is closed with it and later prints fail. On Windows, and on the no-pager path everywhere, the text is written to a temporary file using whatever character set the machine happens to use, so text my terminal can display can still raise an encoding error there.
   6 │ 
   7 │ ## What should happen
   8 │ 
   9 │ Asking for plain output means plain output on every paging path, including the fallback that writes straight to the terminal. Closing what the pager gives me must never close my own output stream. The temporary-file path should write text the same way the pipe path does, using the encoding that matches my output and swapping out characters it cannot represent instead of failing.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## About this project
  12 │ 
  13 │ Click is a Python library for building command line programs. It gives you commands, options, prompts, progress bars, and helpers such as sending long output to a pager like less or more. The pager helper is what makes long help text or long reports easy to scroll through.
  14 │ 
  15 │ ## Problem this solves
  16 │ 
  17 │ I build tools that print long reports, and I need the output to stay readable when it is piped into a file or a log. Right now I get stray colour codes in my saved files, and on Windows my script can crash on text that works everywhere else, so I have to keep text ASCII-only as a workaround.
  18 │ 
  19 │ ## What changed
  20 │ 
  21 │ Colour codes are now removed on the no-pager path too, matching the running-pager path, so the colour setting is honoured everywhere. The stream the pager hands back no longer closes the output underneath it when it is closed itself. The temporary-file path now writes with the same encoding as the pipe path and replaces characters it cannot encode rather than raising an error.
  22 │ 
  23 │ ## Impact

  25 │ Correctness and reliability: plain output is guaranteed on every paging path, my own output stream is safe from being closed, and non-English text no longer fails on Windows.

  70 │   raised `TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'`, and the

class _PagerWriter:
    """Writable text proxy handed to the caller of :func:`get_pager_file`.

    All writes pass through :attr:`stream`, so text is encoded exactly the way
    the pager backend encodes it. Every pager strategy owns the lifecycle of the
    stream it produces; this writer never closes it. ``close()`` flushes and
    stops there, which keeps a borrowed stream such as ``sys.stdout`` usable
    after the caller is done paging, and lets :func:`_pipepager` feed the
    standard error of the pager process as it is produced.

    When ``color`` is false, ANSI color and style codes are removed from each
    write. Stripping happens here rather than in the pager strategies, so the
    ``color`` argument is honored on every paging path, including the fallback
    that writes straight to the output.
    """

    def __init__(self, stream: t.IO[t.Any], color: bool) -> None:
        self.stream = stream
        self.color = color

    def write(self, text: str) -> int:
        if not self.color:
            text = strip_ansi(text)

        rv = self.stream.write(text)
        self.stream.flush()
        return rv

    def flush(self) -> None:
        self.stream.flush()

    def close(self) -> None:
        # Deliberately does not close the stream: the pager that produced it
        # owns its lifecycle, and a borrowed stream must stay open for the
        # caller's later output.
        self.stream.flush()

def _nullpager(
    stream: t.TextIO, color: bool | None = None
) -> t.Iterator[tuple[t.TextIO, str, bool]]:
    """Simply print unformatted text. This is the ultimate fallback. Don't close the
    output stream in this case, since it's coming from elsewhere rather than our
    internal helpers.

    The stream is wrapped in :class:`~click.utils._KeepOpenFile` so that, as a
    borrowed stream, it is not closed by a ``with`` block. The wrapper that
    :func:`get_pager_file` builds around it is detached rather than closed.
    """
    encoding = get_best_encoding(stream)

    if color is None:
        color = False

    yield _KeepOpenFile(stream), encoding, color  # type: ignore[misc]

"""Manual checks for the pager changes described in the ticket."""

import io
import os
import sys

import click
from click import _termui_impl

# 1. No-pager path strips ANSI even for a text-only stream.
stream = io.StringIO()
_termui_impl._default_text_stdout = lambda: stream
_termui_impl.isatty = lambda _: False

with click.get_pager_file(color=False) as pager:
    pager.write(click.style("hello", fg="red"))
print("1 no-pager strip:", repr(stream.getvalue()), "closed:", stream.closed)

# color=True keeps codes.
stream2 = io.StringIO()
_termui_impl._default_text_stdout = lambda: stream2
with click.get_pager_file(color=True) as pager:
    pager.write(click.style("hello", fg="red"))
print("1 no-pager keep: ", repr(stream2.getvalue()))

# 2. Closing the pager stream must not close borrowed stdout.
buf = io.BytesIO()
borrowed = io.TextIOWrapper(buf, encoding="utf-8")
_termui_impl.isatty = lambda _: True
_termui_impl._default_text_stdout = lambda: borrowed
os.environ["PAGER"] = "click-tests-nonexistent-pager-9b3f2"

with click.get_pager_file() as pager:
    pager.write("hello\n")
    pager.close()
    print("2 inside block, stdout closed:", borrowed.closed)

# Later prints still work.
click.echo("still working")
del pager
print("2 after block, stdout closed:", borrowed.closed)
print("2 content:", buf.getvalue())

# 3. Temp file path writes with output encoding and replaces what it cannot encode.
names = []
real = __import__("tempfile").NamedTemporaryFile


def record(*args, **kwargs):
    f = real(*args, **kwargs)
    names.append(kwargs)
    return f


__import__("tempfile").NamedTemporaryFile = record
_termui_impl.WIN = True
_termui_impl.os.environ["PAGER"] = "cat"

click.echo_via_pager("café über", color=False)
print("3 NamedTemporaryFile kwargs:", names[-1])

# Non-encodable text must not raise.
_termui_impl.get_best_encoding = lambda _s: "ascii"
click.echo_via_pager("café über", color=False)
print("3 ascii replace ok")
